description: Milestone 2 Core Mechanics Foundation (Modules 0–6) verified question bank. Every numeric answer is cross-checked by the deterministic mechanics_solvers module. Educational use only — not construction-ready design.

questions.title: Guided Example 0.1 — Convert 5 kNm and 200 GPa to N-mm System
questions.prompt: Following Worked Example 0.1, convert a design bending moment of 5 kN·m into N·mm for direct use with section moduli in mm³.
hints: Step 1: Convert force from kN to N (1 kN = 1,000 N).
Step 2: Convert lever arm from m to mm (1 m = 1,000 mm), giving a combined factor of 1,000 × 1,000 = 10⁶.
questions.solution: 5 kN·m = 5 × (10³ N) × (10³ mm) = 5,000,000 N·mm. Independent check: 5,000,000 N·mm / 10⁶ = 5 kN·m.

questions.title: Independent Example 0.1 — Surface Pressure kN/m² to N/mm²
questions.prompt: Convert an imposed floor pressure of 25 kN/m² into N/mm² (MPa). Enter the numeric value and select the unit.
hints: Write the numerator in N (25 kN = 25,000 N) and the denominator in mm² (1 m² = 1,000,000 mm²).
Divide 25,000 N by 1,000,000 mm².

questions.title: Guided Example 0.2 — Horizontal Component of 20 kN at 35°
questions.prompt: A raking tie exerts a force F = 20 kN inclined at θ = 35° above the horizontal (Example 0.2). Calculate the horizontal force component Fx.
hints: Draw the right-angled force triangle with hypotenuse F = 20 kN and angle 35° to the horizontal axis.
The horizontal component is adjacent to the 35° angle: Fx = F cos(35°).

questions.title: Independent Example 0.2 — Vertical Component of 20 kN at 35°
questions.prompt: For the 20 kN force acting at 35° to the horizontal (Example 0.2), determine the vertical component Fy.
hints: The vertical component is opposite the 35° horizontal angle: Fy = F sin(35°).
Sense check: since 35° < 45°, Fy must be smaller than Fx (16.38 kN).
questions.solution: Fy = 20 × sin(35°) = 20 × 0.57358 = 11.472 kN. Independent check via complementary angle 55°: 20 × cos(55°) = 11.472 kN.

questions.title: 3-4-5 Inclined Strut Lever Arm Concept
questions.prompt: An inclined raking prop with a 3H:4V slope (length 5 m) carries an axial compression F = 50 kN attached at coordinates (x = 3 m, y = 0) relative to pivot O(0,0). How should you compute its moment about O?

options.a: Resolve F at (3 m, 0) into Fx = (3/5)F and Fy = (4/5)F; since Fx passes through y = 0, M_O = Fy × 3 m = 40 kN × 3 m = 120 kNm.
options.b: Multiply the total force 50 kN directly by the 3 m horizontal coordinate to get 150 kNm.
options.c: Multiply the total force 50 kN by the 5 m prop length to get 250 kNm.

hints: Moment equals force multiplied by perpendicular distance to the line of action (or use Varignon's theorem with orthogonal components).
At (3 m, 0), the horizontal component Fx has zero vertical lever arm about (0,0), so only Fy = (4/5)F creates moment about O.
questions.solution: By Varignon's theorem, resolving F at (3 m, 0) gives Fx = 30 kN (line of action passes through O) and Fy = 40 kN at perpendicular distance 3 m, giving M_O = 40 × 3 = 120 kNm.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 0 — Force & Moment Resolution

questions.title: Guided Example 0.3 — Resultant of 8 kN/m UDL over 6 m
questions.prompt: Find the total resultant vertical force W of a uniform load w = 8 kN/m acting over a 6 m span (Example 0.3).
hints: The resultant of a distributed load w(x) is the area under the load intensity diagram: W = ∫ w dx = w × L.
Multiply w = 8 kN/m by L = 6 m.
questions.solution: W = w × L = 8 kN/m × 6 m = 48 kN acting through the centroid at x̄ = L/2 = 3.0 m.

questions.title: Independent Example 0.3 — Static Moment of 8 kN/m UDL about Left Support
questions.prompt: For the 8 kN/m UDL over a 6 m beam (Example 0.3), calculate the static overturning moment M_A of the distributed load about the left support A (x = 0).
hints: First find the resultant force W = 8 × 6 = 48 kN.
Multiply W by the centroidal lever arm x̄ = 6 / 2 = 3.0 m (or evaluate ∫₀⁶ x·w dx = wL²/2).
questions.solution: W = 48 kN acting at x̄ = 3.0 m ⇒ M_A = 48 kN × 3.0 m = 144 kN·m. Independent integral check: ∫₀⁶ 8x dx = [4x²]₀⁶ = 144 kN·m.

questions.title: Calculus Link Between Constant Load, Linear Shear, and Parabolic Moment
questions.prompt: Because dV/dx = -w(x) and dM/dx = V(x), what are the polynomial degrees of the Shear Force Diagram V(x) and Bending Moment Diagram M(x) in a beam region carrying a constant UDL w?

options.a: V(x) is linear (degree 1) with slope -w, and M(x) is parabolic (degree 2) reaching an extremum where V(x) = 0.
options.b: Both V(x) and M(x) are constant horizontal lines across the span.
options.c: V(x) is parabolic (degree 2) and M(x) is linear (degree 1).

hints: Integrating a constant (degree 0) once with respect to x produces a linear function (degree 1).
Integrating a linear function (degree 1) produces a quadratic parabola (degree 2).
questions.solution: Integrating constant w(x) gives linear V(x) = V₀ - wx; integrating linear V(x) gives quadratic (parabolic) M(x) with zero slope dM/dx = 0 where V(x) = 0.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 0 — Visual Calculus for Engineers

questions.title: Guided Example 1.1 — Simply Supported 6 m Beam with 10 kN/m UDL
questions.prompt: A simply supported beam of span L = 6 m carries a uniform load w = 10 kN/m over its full length (Example 1.1). Calculate the vertical support reaction R_A at the left support.
hints: Step 1: Replace the 10 kN/m UDL over 6 m with its resultant W = 10 × 6 = 60 kN at midspan (x = 3 m).
Step 2: Take moments about Support B (ΣM_B = 0): R_A × 6 - 60 × 3 = 0.
questions.solution: Total load W = 60 kN at x̄ = 3 m. ΣM_B = 0 ⇒ R_A = (60 × 3) / 6 = 30 kN; R_B = 30 kN. Independent check: R_A + R_B = 60 kN = W.

questions.title: Guided Example 1.2 — 5 m Beam with 20 kN Load at 2 m from Left Support (R_A)
questions.prompt: A simply supported 5 m beam carries a point load P = 20 kN at distance a = 2 m from left support A (Example 1.2). Calculate the left support reaction R_A.
hints: Distance from the load to right support B is b = 5 - 2 = 3 m.
Take moments about Support B (ΣM_B = 0): -R_A × 5 + 20 × 3 = 0.
questions.solution: ΣM_B = 0 ⇒ R_A = P·b / L = (20 × 3) / 5 = 12.0 kN. Independent check: ΣM_A = 0 ⇒ R_B = (20 × 2) / 5 = 8.0 kN, and R_A + R_B = 12 + 8 = 20 kN.

questions.title: Independent Example 1.2 — Combined UDL and Eccentric Point Load Reactions
questions.prompt: A simply supported 5 m beam carries BOTH a full-span UDL w = 6 kN/m AND a 20 kN point load at 2 m from left support A. Calculate the total vertical reaction R_A at left support A.
hints: Total UDL resultant W = 6 × 5 = 30 kN acting at x = 2.5 m; point load P = 20 kN acts at x = 2.0 m.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 1 — Superposition of Beam Reactions

questions.title: Guided Example 1.3 — One-Way Floor Bay Tributary Line Load
questions.prompt: A one-way spanning floor bay measures 4 m (slab span) × 5 m (beam span) with dead load g_k = 1.0 kN/m² and live load q_k = 1.5 kN/m² (Example 1.3). Calculate the total characteristic line load w on one supporting 5 m edge beam.
hints: Step 1: The slab spans 4 m one-way between two 5 m beams, so each edge beam has a tributary width b_trib = 4 m / 2 = 2.0 m.
Step 2: Multiply the combined area pressure (1.0 + 1.5 = 2.5 kN/m²) by the 2.0 m tributary width.
questions.solution: b_trib = 4.0 / 2 = 2.0 m. Line load w = (g_k + q_k) × b_trib = (1.0 + 1.5) kN/m² × 2.0 m = 5.0 kN/m. Independent check: Total bay load = 2.5 × (4×5) = 50 kN; two 5 m beams carry 2 × (5.0 × 5) = 50 kN.

questions.title: Independent Example 1.3 — Edge Beam End Reaction from Floor Bay
questions.prompt: For the 5 m simply supported edge beam in Example 1.3 carrying the tributary line load w = 5.0 kN/m from the 4 m × 5 m floor bay, calculate the vertical force delivered to one supporting corner column at the end of the beam.
hints: Total load on the 5 m edge beam is W_beam = w × L_beam = 5.0 kN/m × 5.0 m = 25.0 kN.
Each end support of the simply supported 5 m beam carries half of W_beam (which also equals 1/4 of the 50 kN floor bay).
questions.solution: R_col = w × L_beam / 2 = 5.0 × 5.0 / 2 = 12.5 kN. Independent tributary-area check: One corner column supports a quadrant of 2.0 m × 2.5 m = 5.0 m² at 2.5 kN/m² = 12.5 kN.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 1 — Example 1.3 Load Path Takedown

questions.title: Static Determinacy and Mechanism Identification in Pin-Jointed Frames
questions.prompt: A single-bay rectangular steel frame has four pin joints (at both column bases and both beam-to-column corners) and no diagonal bracing or shear wall. How does this frame behave under a horizontal wind load?

options.a: It is a mechanism (unstable sway collapse): with four pins in a rectangular loop and no diagonal or moment restraint, it offers zero horizontal stiffness.
options.b: It is statically determinate and stable because it has two pin base supports providing four reaction components.
options.c: It is statically indeterminate to degree 1 because both column bases are pinned.

hints: Check whether the rectangular four-bar linkage can deform laterally without any member changing length.
Without a diagonal brace, shear infill, or moment-resisting knee joint, the frame sways freely as a four-hinge mechanism.
questions.solution: A rectangular frame with pinned bases and pinned beam-to-column connections is a four-hinge sway mechanism with zero lateral stiffness; stability requires diagonal bracing, a shear core, or moment-resisting joints.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 1 — Stability vs Mechanism

questions.title: Guided Example 2.1 — Internal Shear and Moment by Method of Sections at Quarter-Span
questions.prompt: For the simply supported 6 m beam carrying w = 10 kN/m (Example 2.1, R_A = 30 kN), make a section cut at x = 1.5 m from left support A and calculate the internal sagging bending moment M(1.5 m).
hints: Isolate the left 1.5 m segment: upward reaction R_A = 30 kN at x = 0, and downward UDL on the cut segment = 10 × 1.5 = 15 kN acting at 0.75 m from the cut.
Sum moments about the cut at x = 1.5 m: M(1.5) = 30 × 1.5 - 15 × 0.75.
questions.solution: M(1.5) = R_A(1.5) - w(1.5)²/2 = 45.0 - 11.25 = 33.75 kN·m (sagging). Independent shear-area check: V(0) = 30 kN, V(1.5) = 15 kN; trapezoid area = ½(30 + 15) × 1.5 = 33.75 kN·m.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 2 — Example 2.1 Method of Sections

questions.title: UK Structural Sign Convention for Internal Shear and Sagging/Hogging Moment
questions.prompt: When you make an imaginary vertical cut through a horizontal beam and isolate the left-hand segment, which internal action directions correspond to positive shear (+V) and positive bending moment (+M) in UK structural practice?

options.a: Positive shear (+V) acts downward on the right face of the left-hand segment (balancing an upward left reaction), and positive sagging moment (+M) puts the bottom extreme fibre in tension.
options.b: Positive bending moment (+M) always puts the top flange in tension regardless of support conditions.
options.c: Internal shear V and moment M are global external reactions and do not require a section cut to expose.

hints: Consider a left support with an upward reaction R_A: to hold the left slice in vertical equilibrium, the internal shear on the cut face must point downward.
Sagging bends the beam concave-upward (smiling), stretching the bottom fibres in tension.
questions.solution: Under the standard UK convention, upward force on the left segment is balanced by a downward internal shear V on the cut face (+V), and positive bending moment (+M, sagging) causes tension in the bottom face.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 2 — Internal Action Sign Conventions

questions.title: Internal Axial, Shear, and Moment at Mid-Span of Cantilever with Inclined Tip Load
questions.prompt: A horizontal 2.0 m cantilever fixed at A (x = 0) carries a downward vertical load of 8 kN and a horizontal tensile pull of 6 kN at its free tip B (x = 2.0 m). Calculate the magnitude of the internal hogging bending moment at the midpoint x = 1.0 m.
hints: Cut the cantilever at x = 1.0 m and isolate the free right-hand segment from x = 1.0 m to x = 2.0 m (length 1.0 m).
The concentric 6 kN axial pull passes through the centroidal axis (zero lever arm), so only the 8 kN vertical tip load with lever arm 1.0 m creates bending moment.
questions.solution: Isolating the 1.0 m free-end segment: N = +6 kN (tension), V = +8 kN, and |M(1.0 m)| = 8 kN × 1.0 m = 8.0 kN·m (hogging, top face in tension).
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 2 — Method of Sections

questions.title: Guided Example 2.1 — Maximum Sagging Moment of 6 m Beam with 10 kN/m UDL
questions.prompt: For the simply supported 6 m beam carrying a full-span UDL w = 10 kN/m (Example 2.1), calculate the maximum sagging bending moment M_max at midspan.
hints: Shear crosses zero at midspan x = 3.0 m where R_A = 30 kN.
Calculate M_max = R_A(3.0) - (10 × 3.0)(1.5) = wL²/8, or take the area of the positive shear triangle ½ × 30 kN × 3.0 m.
questions.solution: M_max = wL²/8 = 10 × 6² / 8 = 45.0 kN·m (sagging, tension in bottom face). Independent check via shear triangle area: ½ × 30 kN × 3.0 m = 45.0 kN·m.

questions.title: Guided Example 2.2 — Fixed-End Hogging Moment Magnitude of 2 m Cantilever with 5 kN/m UDL
questions.prompt: A 2 m cantilever beam carries a uniform downward load w = 5 kN/m over its full length (Example 2.2). Calculate the magnitude of the fixed-end bending moment |M_fixed| at the support.
hints: Total downward load on the 2 m cantilever is W = 5 × 2 = 10 kN acting at centroid x̄ = 1.0 m from the fixed root.
|M_fixed| = W × x̄ = wL²/2.
questions.solution: |M_fixed| = wL²/2 = 5 × 2² / 2 = 10.0 kN·m (hogging: M = -10.0 kN·m, placing the top face in tension). Independent check via shear triangle area: ½ × 10 kN × 2.0 m = 10.0 kN·m.

questions.title: Tension Face Identification in Cantilever vs Simply Supported Beams
questions.prompt: In UK structural detailing where Bending Moment Diagrams are plotted on the tension face of the member, where is the BMD plotted for (1) a simply supported beam under gravity load and (2) a cantilever under gravity load?

options.a: Below the beam axis (bottom face in tension, sagging) for the simply supported beam, and above the beam axis (top face in tension, hogging) for the cantilever.
options.b: Above the beam axis for both beams because gravity loads always act downward.
options.c: Below the beam axis for both beams because maximum moment is always positive.

hints: Visualise how each beam deflects under downward gravity load.
A simply supported beam sags (stretching the bottom face), whereas a cantilever droops downward at the tip (stretching the top face over the support).
questions.solution: Plotting BMD on the tension face immediately shows where tensile reinforcement (in RC) or tensile flange restraint is required: bottom face for sagging simply supported spans, top face for hogging cantilevers.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 2 — Tension-Side BMD Convention

questions.title: Guided Example 2.3 — Peak Bending Moment for 5 m Beam with 20 kN Load at 2 m
questions.prompt: A simply supported 5 m beam carries an eccentric point load P = 20 kN at a = 2 m from left support A (Example 2.3, R_A = 12 kN, R_B = 8 kN). Calculate the maximum sagging bending moment M_max.
hints: Do NOT use PL/4 because the point load is off-centre (a = 2 m, b = 3 m).
The shear steps from +12 kN to -8 kN at x = 2 m, so M_max occurs directly under the load: M_max = R_A × a = 12 kN × 2 m.
questions.solution: M_max = P·a·b / L = R_A × a = 12.0 kN × 2.0 m = 24.0 kN·m. Independent right-hand cut check: R_B × b = 8.0 kN × 3.0 m = 24.0 kN·m.

questions.title: Independent Asymmetric Beam — Locating Zero Shear and Peak Moment
questions.prompt: A simply supported 6 m beam carries a uniform load w = 10 kN/m AND an eccentric point load P = 15 kN at x = 2 m from left support A (giving R_A = 40 kN and R_B = 35 kN). Locate where shear V(x) crosses zero (x = 2.5 m) and calculate the true maximum sagging bending moment M_max.
hints: Step 1: Just right of x = 2 m, V(2⁺) = 40 - 10(2) - 15 = +5 kN. Shear continues decreasing at 10 kN/m and crosses zero at x = 2.0 + 5/10 = 2.5 m.
questions.solution: Zero shear occurs at x = 2.5 m (since V(2.5) = 40 - 10(2.5) - 15 = 0). Evaluating moment at x = 2.5 m gives M_max = 40(2.5) - 5(6.25) - 15(0.5) = 100 - 31.25 - 7.50 = 61.25 kN·m. Independent right-hand cut check: R_B(3.5) - 10(3.5)²/2 = 122.5 - 61.25 = 61.25 kN·m.

questions.title: Effect of an Applied Concentrated Couple on SFD and BMD
questions.prompt: A horizontal beam carries an externally applied concentrated moment (couple) M₀ = 15 kNm welded to a bracket at midspan. What local discontinuity does M₀ produce in the Shear Force Diagram (SFD) and Bending Moment Diagram (BMD)?

options.a: No jump in the SFD (since a pure couple has zero net vertical force), and an immediate vertical step discontinuity of 15 kNm in the BMD.
options.b: A vertical step of 15 kN in the SFD and a slope change in the BMD.
options.c: No change in either the SFD or the BMD at the point of application.

hints: Apply vertical force equilibrium ΣF_y = 0 across an infinitesimal slice Δx straddling the applied couple.
Apply moment equilibrium ΣM = 0 across the same infinitesimal slice Δx.
questions.solution: A pure couple adds zero vertical force (ΔV = 0, so the SFD does not jump), whereas rotational equilibrium across an infinitesimal slice produces an immediate step ΔM = M₀ in the BMD.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 2 — Concentrated Couples on Beams

questions.title: Overhanging Beam Support Hogging Moment
questions.prompt: A beam is supported at A (x = 0) and B (x = 4 m) and cantilevers 1.5 m past B to a free tip C (x = 5.5 m). If the overhang BC carries a vertical tip load P = 12 kN at C, calculate the magnitude of the hogging bending moment |M_B| over support B.
hints: Cut the beam just to the right of support B and isolate the 1.5 m overhanging cantilever segment BC.
Multiply the 12 kN tip load at C by the 1.5 m overhang lever arm.
questions.solution: Isolating overhang BC: |M_B| = 12 kN × 1.5 m = 18.0 kN·m (hogging over support B, top face in tension). Independent check via left span AB: ΣM_A = 0 ⇒ R_B(4) - 12(5.5) = 0 ⇒ R_B = 16.5 kN, R_A = -4.5 kN (tie-down), so M_B = R_A × 4 = -18.0 kN·m.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 2 — Overhanging Beams & Contraflexure

questions.title: Locating Point of Contraflexure in a Beam with Overhang
questions.prompt: A beam supported at A (x = 0) and B (x = 4 m) with a 1 m overhang to C (x = 5 m) carries a uniform load w = 8 kN/m over its entire 5 m length (giving R_A = 15 kN upward and R_B = 25 kN upward). At what non-zero distance x (in m) from support A does the point of contraflexure (M(x) = 0) occur inside span AB?
hints: Write the bending moment equation inside span AB (0 < x ≤ 4 m): M(x) = R_A x - w x² / 2 = 15x - 4x².
Set M(x) = x(15 - 4x) = 0 and solve for the non-zero root x = 15 / 4.
questions.solution: For 0 < x ≤ 4 m, M(x) = 15x - 4x² = x(15 - 4x) = 0 ⇒ x = 15 / 4 = 3.75 m. At x = 3.75 m, bending transitions from sagging (+M) to hogging (-M, reaching -4.0 kN·m over support B).
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 2 — Points of Contraflexure

questions.title: Physical Meaning of a Point of Contraflexure
questions.prompt: What happens structurally at a point of contraflexure (inflection point) along a continuous or overhanging beam?

options.a: The internal bending moment M(x) passes through zero and changes sign between sagging and hogging, so curvature reverses and tension switches from one face of the beam to the other.
options.b: The internal shear force V(x) is necessarily zero and the bending moment reaches its maximum value.
options.c: The vertical deflection δ(x) of the beam is guaranteed to be zero.

hints: Recall the curvature-moment relation κ = M / (EI).
When M = 0, curvature κ = 0 as the beam transitions from concave-up (sagging) to concave-down (hogging).
questions.solution: At a point of contraflexure, M(x) = 0 and changes sign; curvature reverses and the tensile face switches between top and bottom (while shear V(x) is generally non-zero).

questions.title: Guided Example 3.1 — Elongation of 3 m Steel Tie under 100 kN Tension
questions.prompt: A steel tie of length L = 3 m (3,000 mm) and area A = 1,000 mm² carries a tensile force F = 100 kN with E = 200 GPa (Example 3.1). Calculate the axial elongation ΔL.
hints: Step 1: Direct stress σ = F/A = 100,000 N / 1,000 mm² = 100 MPa (N/mm²).
Step 2: Strain ε = σ/E = 100 / 200,000 = 0.0005; Elongation ΔL = εL = 0.0005 × 3,000 mm.
questions.solution: σ = 100 MPa, ε = 0.0005, ΔL = FL/(EA) = (100,000 × 3,000) / (200,000 × 1,000) = 1.50 mm. Independent energy check: ½ F ΔL = 75,000 N·mm = ½ σ ε (AL).

questions.title: Guided Example 3.2 — Steel vs Aluminium Extension Ratio
questions.prompt: A steel bar (E_steel = 210 GPa) and an aluminium bar (E_al = 70 GPa) have identical length L = 2,000 mm and area A = 500 mm² and carry the same axial tensile load F = 50 kN (Example 3.2). What is the ratio of the aluminium bar's extension to the steel bar's extension (ΔL_al / ΔL_steel)?
hints: Since F, L, and A are identical for both bars, the direct stress σ = F/A = 100 MPa is identical in both bars.
Extension ΔL = σL / E is inversely proportional to E: ΔL_al / ΔL_steel = E_steel / E_al.
questions.solution: ΔL_steel = 0.9524 mm, ΔL_al = 2.8571 mm ⇒ ΔL_al / ΔL_steel = E_steel / E_al = 210 / 70 = 3.0.

questions.title: Distinguishing Material Stiffness (E), Strength (f_y, f_u), and Ductility
questions.prompt: Which statement accurately distinguishes Young's modulus (E), yield strength (f_y), and ductility in structural steel?

options.a: Young's modulus E is the initial elastic slope of the stress–strain curve governing elastic stiffness; yield strength f_y is the stress at which permanent plastic strain begins; ductility is the ability to undergo large plastic strain before fracture.
options.b: S355 steel has a significantly higher Young's modulus E than S275 steel, making it deflect less in the elastic range.
options.c: Brittle materials have a large plastic yield plateau before sudden fracture.

hints: Compare the elastic slope E (≈ 210 GPa for both S275 and S355) with the yield plateau stress f_y (275 MPa vs 355 MPa).
Ductility measures post-yield plastic deformation capacity, which allows local stress redistribution and warning before failure.
questions.solution: E governs elastic deformation per unit stress (identical at ~210 GPa across S235/S275/S355), f_y marks the onset of yielding, and ductility provides plastic deformation capacity and warning prior to fracture.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 3 — Stiffness, Strength & Ductility

questions.title: Centroid Height of an Asymmetric Tee Section
questions.prompt: A welded steel Tee section consists of a bottom web 10 mm wide × 150 mm tall (0 ≤ y ≤ 150 mm) and a top flange 150 mm wide × 20 mm thick (150 ≤ y ≤ 170 mm). Calculate the height ȳ of the section centroid measured from the bottom edge (y = 0).
hints: Web area A₁ = 10 × 150 = 1,500 mm² with centroid y₁ = 75 mm; Flange area A₂ = 150 × 20 = 3,000 mm² with centroid y₂ = 150 + 10 = 160 mm.
Calculate ȳ = (A₁ y₁ + A₂ y₂) / (A₁ + A₂).
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 4 — Centroids & Neutral Axis

questions.title: First Moment of Area Q at the Neutral Axis of a 75 mm × 225 mm Timber Joist
questions.prompt: For the 75 mm wide × 225 mm deep rectangular timber joist in Example 4.1, calculate the First Moment of Area Q_NA of the half-section above the neutral axis about the neutral axis.
hints: The half-section above the neutral axis has width b = 75 mm and height h_half = 225 / 2 = 112.5 mm.
Its centroid lies at y_c = h_half / 2 = 56.25 mm above the neutral axis, so Q_NA = A_half × y_c = b d² / 8.
questions.solution: Q_NA = (75 × 112.5) × 56.25 = 8,437.5 mm² × 56.25 mm = 474,609.375 mm³ (= bd²/8). Note that Q_NA (bd²/8) is physically distinct from W_el (bd²/6 = 632,812.5 mm³).
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 4 — First Moment of Area Q vs Section Modulus W_el

questions.title: Semantic Distinction Between First Moment of Area Q and Elastic Section Modulus W_el
questions.prompt: Both First Moment of Area (Q) and Elastic Section Modulus (W_el or Z) have units of mm³ (L³). Why is it a conceptual error to substitute Q into the bending stress formula σ = M / W_el?

options.a: Q = ∫ y dA is the area moment of a specific sub-region used in shear stress (τ = VQ / Ib), whereas W_el = I / y_max is the whole-section flexural modulus relating bending moment M to extreme-fibre normal stress.
options.b: Q and W_el have identical values for all cross-sections, so substituting Q gives the same bending stress.
options.c: Q has units of mm⁴ whereas W_el has units of mm³.

hints: Compare the definitions: Q = A_slice × ȳ_slice (for a rectangle at the NA, bd²/8) versus W_el = I / (d/2) (for a rectangle, bd²/6).
Dimensional equality (both L³) does not imply physical equivalence.
questions.solution: Although both have dimension L³ (mm³), Q measures the statical moment of an area slice above a shear plane (τ = VQ/Ib), whereas W_el = I / y_max governs extreme-fibre bending stress (σ = M / W_el).
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 4 — Semantic Quantity Distinctions

questions.title: Guided Example 4.1 — Bending Stress in 75 mm × 225 mm Timber Joist under 8 kNm
questions.prompt: A rectangular timber joist of width b = 75 mm and depth d = 225 mm carries a bending moment M = 8 kN·m (Example 4.1). Calculate the maximum elastic bending stress σ_max.
hints: Step 1: Calculate elastic section modulus W_el = bd²/6 = 75 × 225² / 6 = 632,812.5 mm³.
Step 2: Convert M = 8 kN·m = 8,000,000 N·mm and compute σ = M / W_el.
questions.solution: W_el = 75 × 225² / 6 = 632,812.5 mm³. σ = 8,000,000 N·mm / 632,812.5 mm³ = 12.642 MPa. Increasing depth to 300 mm raises W_el to 1,125,000 mm³ and lowers σ to 7.111 MPa.

questions.title: Guided Example 4.2 — Parallel Axis Theorem for Welded Symmetric I-Section
questions.prompt: A symmetric I-section is built from two 150 mm × 20 mm flanges and a 200 mm × 10 mm web (overall depth H = 240 mm, Example 4.2). Calculate the major-axis Second Moment of Area I_xx.
hints: Web inertia: I_web = 10 × 200³ / 12 = 6,666,666.7 mm⁴.
Each flange has A_f = 150 × 20 = 3,000 mm² at centroidal offset d_f = 100 + 10 = 110 mm from the NA: 2 × [150×20³/12 + 3,000×110²] = 72,800,000 mm⁴.

questions.title: Independent Example 4.3 — UB Major vs Minor Axis Stiffness Ratio (Supplied Properties)
questions.prompt: [Reference Verification Note: Geometric properties are explicitly supplied here; verify actual rolled section properties against an SCI Blue Book table.] For a Universal Beam with supplied properties I_y = 21,500 cm⁴ (major axis, web vertical) and I_z = 1,200 cm⁴ (minor axis, web horizontal), calculate the ratio of major-axis to minor-axis flexural stiffness (I_y / I_z).
hints: Since Young's modulus E is identical in both orientations, the flexural stiffness ratio (EI_y)/(EI_z) equals I_y / I_z.
Divide 21,500 cm⁴ by 1,200 cm⁴.
questions.solution: I_y / I_z = 21,500 / 1,200 = 17.917. Orienting the UB with its web vertical provides nearly 18 times the flexural stiffness of laying it flat.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 4 — Example 4.3 (Reference Verification Required for Rolled Tables)

questions.title: Independent Example 4.4 — Plastic vs Elastic Shape Factor of a Rectangular Section
questions.prompt: For a rectangular cross-section of width b and depth d (Example 4.4), why is the plastic section modulus W_pl = bd²/4 exactly 1.5 times the elastic section modulus W_el = bd²/6?

options.a: At first yield (M_el), only the extreme top and bottom fibres reach f_y (triangular stress distribution with lever arm ⅔d), whereas at full plasticity (M_pl) the entire top and bottom halves yield at ±f_y (rectangular blocks with lever arm ½d and double the average stress).
options.b: Because the material's Young's modulus E increases by 50% once yielding begins.
options.c: Because the neutral axis shifts to the top edge of the rectangle under pure bending.

hints: Compare the internal force of a triangular stress block (½ f_y × bd/2) at lever arm ⅔d with a rectangular stress block (f_y × bd/2) at lever arm ½d.
The ratio of moments is (1 × ½) / (½ × ⅔) = (1/2) / (1/3) = 1.50.
questions.solution: In elastic bending, stress varies linearly from 0 at the NA to f_y at the extreme fibre (M_el = f_y bd²/6). In full plastic bending, all fibres yield at ±f_y (M_pl = f_y bd²/4), giving a shape factor W_pl / W_el = 1.50.

questions.title: Guided Example 5.1 — Midspan Deflection Factor When Span Increases from 4 m to 5 m
questions.prompt: A simply supported beam carries a uniform load w over span L (Example 5.1, δ_max = 5wL⁴ / 384EI). If the span increases from 4 m to 5 m while w, E, and I remain unchanged, by what factor (δ₅ / δ₄) does the midspan deflection increase?
hints: For a uniform load w (kN/m), midspan deflection scales with the FOURTH power of span: δ ∝ L⁴.
Compute (5 / 4)⁴ = 1.25⁴.
questions.solution: δ₅ / δ₄ = (5 / 4)⁴ = 1.25⁴ = 2.4414. A 25% increase in span increases UDL deflection by 144.1%!

questions.title: Independent Example 5.1 — Midspan Deflection of 4 m Steel Beam under 12 kN/m
questions.prompt: Calculate the elastic midspan deflection δ_max = 5wL⁴ / (384EI) of a simply supported 4.0 m steel beam (E = 210 GPa, I = 66.667 × 10⁶ mm⁴) carrying an unfactored serviceability UDL w = 12 kN/m (Example 5.1 baseline).
hints: Convert to consistent N-mm units: w = 12 kN/m = 12 N/mm; L = 4,000 mm; E = 210,000 N/mm²; I = 66,666,667 mm⁴.
questions.solution: Numerator = 5 × 12 × 2.56×10¹⁴ = 1.536×10¹⁶ N·mm⁴. Denominator = 384 × 210,000 × 66,666,667 = 5.376×10¹⁵ N·mm³. δ_max = 2.857 mm (Span/1400, well within L/360 = 11.1 mm).

questions.title: Why Upgrading Steel Grade from S275 to S355 Does Not Fix Excessive Elastic Deflection
questions.prompt: A floor beam satisfies Ultimate Limit State (ULS) bending strength checks in S275 steel, but fails the Serviceability Limit State (SLS) deflection limit. What happens to the elastic deflection if the engineer changes the steel grade from S275 to S355 while keeping the same UB section size?

options.a: The elastic deflection remains completely unchanged (0% reduction) because S275 and S355 steels have the same Young's modulus E = 210 GPa; increasing section depth or I is required instead.
options.b: The elastic deflection decreases by 29% in proportion to the yield strength ratio 275 / 355.
options.c: The elastic deflection is halved because higher-grade steel has double the second moment of area I.

hints: Inspect the elastic deflection formula δ = 5wL⁴ / (384EI): does yield strength f_y appear anywhere in the formula?
Both S275 and S355 have E = 210 GPa, so changing steel grade does not alter EI.
questions.solution: Elastic deflection depends on flexural rigidity EI, not yield strength f_y. Because E = 210 GPa for both S275 and S355, changing grade produces zero reduction in elastic deflection; a deeper or heavier section (larger I) must be chosen.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 5 — Example 5.1 Stiffness vs Strength

questions.title: Guided Example 6.1 — Theoretical Euler Buckling Load of 4 m Pinned-Pinned Column
questions.prompt: Calculate the theoretical elastic Euler buckling load P_cr = π²EI / L_cr² for a 4.0 m pinned-pinned steel column (L_cr = 1.0 L = 4,000 mm, E = 210 GPa, minor-axis I = 8.0 × 10⁶ mm⁴, Example 6.1).
hints: Work in N and mm: E = 210,000 N/mm², I = 8,000,000 mm⁴, L_cr = 4,000 mm.
Calculate P_cr = π² × 210,000 × 8,000,000 / 4,000² in N, then divide by 1,000 to convert to kN.
questions.solution: P_cr = π² × 210,000 × 8.0×10⁶ / (4,000)² = 1,036,308.5 N = 1,036.31 kN. Independent slenderness check (for A = 2,500 mm²): i = √(I/A) = 56.57 mm, λ = 70.71, σ_cr = 414.52 MPa ⇒ P_cr = σ_cr A = 1,036.31 kN.

questions.title: Independent Example 6.1 — Fixed-Fixed vs Pinned-Pinned Euler Buckling Ratio
questions.prompt: In Example 6.1, if the ends of the 4.0 m column are changed from pinned-pinned (L_cr = 1.0 L) to theoretically fixed-fixed against rotation and sway (L_cr = 0.5 L), what is the theoretical fixed-fixed Euler buckling load P_cr,fixed?
hints: Halving the effective buckling length L_cr from 4,000 mm to 2,000 mm divides the denominator L_cr² by 0.5² = 0.25.
Multiply the pinned-pinned Euler load (1,036.31 kN) by 4.
questions.solution: With L_cr = 0.5 L = 2,000 mm, P_cr,fixed = π²EI / (0.5L)² = 4 × P_cr,pinned = 4 × 1,036.31 = 4,145.23 kN.

questions.title: Why Real Structural Columns Buckle Below the Theoretical Euler Load P_cr
questions.prompt: Why do real rolled steel columns in buildings and temporary works propping fail at compressive loads significantly below the theoretical elastic Euler buckling load P_cr = π²EI / L_cr²?

options.a: Real columns have initial geometric bow (out-of-straightness), load eccentricities, residual thermal stresses from rolling/welding, and inelastic material yielding at intermediate slenderness.
options.b: Because Euler's derivation assumes concrete rather than structural steel.
options.c: Because real columns always buckle about their major axis (I_y) instead of their minor axis (I_z).

hints: Recall the idealisations in Euler's derivation: perfectly straight axis, perfectly concentric load, zero residual stress, and unlimited linear-elastic stress.
In reality, initial bow e₀ and residual stresses trigger combined compression + P-δ bending and early flange yielding.
questions.solution: Real columns exhibit initial geometric imperfections (bow), unintended load eccentricity, residual stresses, and finite yield strength f_y—all of which reduce buckling resistance below the ideal elastic Euler curve.
questions.reference: Master Syllabus Module 6 — Ideal Euler vs Real Column Behaviour
